name: Myofibrillar hypertrophy training

lead: Myofibrillar hypertrophy is growth in the contractile proteins (actin and myosin) of muscle fibres. Training for it means heavy loads and progressive overload, often with lower reps and longer rests, so that muscles get both bigger and stronger.

For appearance, the payoff is more muscle on the frame, shoulders, chest, back and legs, together with strength gains. A 2019 Sports Medicine editorial argues exercise-induced myofibrillar hypertrophy contributes to strength gains.[1]

paras: Lifters build programs around heavy compound lifts with progressive overload, sometimes contrasted with higher-rep "bodybuilding" work. Many combine both, since the two kinds of growth rarely occur independently.[2]

Heavy lifting carries ordinary injury risk (joints, tendons, lower back) and is commonly done with warm-ups and technique focus. The idea that heavy and light training grow different parts of the fibre is itself debated.

chain: Growth of contractile proteins in muscle fibres
More and denser-looking muscle, plus strength
angle.text: Heavy-load training is used to add muscle mass and strength. The extra muscle shows up as a fuller, more developed physique.

lead: Myofibrillar hypertrophy refers to growth in the contractile proteins actin and myosin, which adds strength along with some size; it is contrasted with sarcoplasmic hypertrophy, an increase in fluid and glycogen storage in the muscle cell.[1] The idea that bodybuilders mainly show sarcoplasmic growth and Olympic weightlifters myofibrillar growth is widespread in lifting circles.[1]

People who train for it use heavy loads and progressive overload to build a dense, strong physique. Forum discussions on T Nation ask what the main driver of muscle growth is and how heavy training compares with volume.[2]

The split is disputed: Wikipedia's article states that it comes largely from the bodybuilding community and that its evidence needs qualification, and notes that the two forms rarely occur fully independently.[1] A 2019 editorial argues that myofibrillar hypertrophy contributes to strength gains.[3]

paras: Strength training produces neural adaptations that account for much of early strength gain and also drives muscle growth through added sarcomeres and sarcoplasmic fluid.[1] Load and intensity matter for hypertrophy, and very slow tempos can limit the load lifted.[1]
Lifters on forums debate whether heavy work, volume, tempo or soreness drives growth, and some argue that scientific detail matters little compared with training consistently.[2][4]

The Wikipedia overview calls the sarcoplasmic/myofibrillar split disputed and reports conflicting studies on tempo and time under tension.[1] An editorial in Sports Medicine argues myofibrillar hypertrophy is a contributory cause of strength gains.[3]
Direct human trials separating the two hypertrophy types are limited. The editorial addresses their link to strength gains.[3]

lore.intro: Forum threads discuss what drives muscle growth, with different camps on load, volume and soreness.[2][4]

claims.claim: Heavy low-rep training builds dense, strength-oriented muscle, while high-rep work builds only fluid size.
